claim: CRISPR-Cas systems provide bacteria and archaea with programmable immunity against mobile genetic elements.
source: CRISPR-Cas systems provide bacteria and archaea with programmable immunity against mobile genetic elements.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Bacteriophage have evolved small protein inhibitors called anti-CRISPRs (Acrs) that block Cas enzyme function.
source: Evolutionary pressure by CRISPR-Cas has driven bacteriophage to evolve small protein inhibitors, anti-CRISPRs (Acrs), that block Cas enzyme function by wide-ranging mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: AcrVA4 recognizes the L. bacterium Cas12a (LbCas12a) pre-crRNA processing nuclease and forms a Cas12a dimer.
source: We show here that the inhibitor AcrVA4 uses a previously undescribed strategy to recognize the L. bacterium Cas12a (LbCas12a) pre-crRNA processing nuclease, forming a Cas12a dimer, and allosterically inhibiting DNA binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including cryo-EM structures.

claim: AcrVA4 allosterically inhibits DNA binding by Cas12a.
source: We show here that the inhibitor AcrVA4 uses a previously undescribed strategy to recognize the L. bacterium Cas12a (LbCas12a) pre-crRNA processing nuclease, forming a Cas12a dimer, and allosterically inhibiting DNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays and structural data showing AcrVA4 binding away from the DNA binding site.

claim: AsCas12a contains an ancestral helical bundle that blocks AcrVA4 binding.
source: The Ac. species Cas12a (AsCas12a) enzyme, widely used for genome editing applications, contains an ancestral helical bundle that blocks AcrVA4 binding and allows it to escape anti-CRISPR recognition.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and phylogenetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cas12a orthologs can be rendered either sensitive or resistant to AcrVA4 through rational structural engineering.
source: Using biochemical, microbiological, and human cell editing experiments, we show that Cas12a orthologs can be rendered either sensitive or resistant to AcrVA4 through rational structural engineering informed by evolution.
evidence: This is demonstrated through chimeric protein experiments in vitro, in bacteria, and in human cells.

claim: Cas12a directly catalyzes precursor crRNA (pre-crRNA) processing to generate a mature surveillance complex.
source: Unlike Cas9, Cas12a directly catalyzes precursor crRNA (pre-crRNA) processing to generate a mature surveillance complex whose crRNA bears a hydroxyl on its 5' terminus (Zetsche et al., 2015; Fonfara et al., 2016; Swarts et al., 2017) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mature crRNA produced by Cas12a processing bears a hydroxyl on its 5' terminus.
source: Unlike Cas9, Cas12a directly catalyzes precursor crRNA (pre-crRNA) processing to generate a mature surveillance complex whose crRNA bears a hydroxyl on its 5' terminus (Zetsche et al., 2015; Fonfara et al., 2016; Swarts et al., 2017) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AcrVA4 is 234 amino acids in length, almost twice as large as other anti-CRISPR proteins.
source: At 234 amino acids, AcrVA4 is almost twice as large as other anti-CRISPR proteins and it contains a predicted coiled-coil domain not observed in other Acrs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence analysis.

claim: AcrVA4 contains a predicted coiled-coil domain not observed in other Acrs.
source: At 234 amino acids, AcrVA4 is almost twice as large as other anti-CRISPR proteins and it contains a predicted coiled-coil domain not observed in other Acrs.
evidence: This is based on structural prediction and analysis.

claim: AcrVA4's mode of action involves dimerization of Cas12a.
source: In addition, similar to specific Acrs that target Cas9 (Harrington et al., 2017) or Cas10 (He et al., 2018), its mode of action appears to involve dimerization of Cas12a (Knott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited and structural data in this manuscript.

claim: The structure of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex bound to AcrVA4 was determined at 3.0 Å resolution using cryo-EM.
source: From a subset of 156,979 particle images identified by three-dimensional classification, we reconstructed a three dimensional cryo-EM density map at 3.0 Å resolution (State I) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the cryo-EM experiment.

claim: The C-terminal domain of AcrVA4 (residues 136–233) was resolved in the cryo-EM structure.
source: The map contained additional density not attributable to LbCas12a-crRNA that allowed for unambiguous de novo tracing and sequence register assignment of the C-terminal domain of AcrVA4 (residues 136–233) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The PAM-interacting (PI) domain of LbCas12a was disordered in the cryo-EM structure.
source: With the exception of the PAM-interacting (PI) domain, which was disordered in our structure, we resolved most of the LbCas12a protein and crRNA to high-resolution (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The CBD of AcrVA4 adopts a compact ɑ1β1-β5ɑ2 fold.
source: Residues 136–233 of AcrVA4 adopt a compact ɑ1β1-β5ɑ2 fold, defined here as the C-terminal binding domain (CBD), that forms an extensive interface with LbCas12a (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The buried surface area between AcrVA4 and LbCas12a is 1479 Å2, accounting for 23.8% of the total solvent accessible surface area of the CBD.
source: The 1479 Å2 of buried surface area between AcrVA4 and LbCas12a accounts for 23.8% of the total solvent accessible surface area of the CBD.
evidence: This is calculated from the structural data.

claim: AcrVA4 exists as an obligate dimer in solution.
source: While the CBD of only a single copy of AcrVA4 was well resolved in State I, AcrVA4 exists as an obligate dimer in solution that binds directly to either one or two copies of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex (Knott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by previous work and SEC-SAXS data in this manuscript.

claim: AcrVA4 binds directly to either one or two copies of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex.
source: While the CBD of only a single copy of AcrVA4 was well resolved in State I, AcrVA4 exists as an obligate dimer in solution that binds directly to either one or two copies of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex (Knott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by previous work and structural data showing both monomeric and dimeric complexes.

claim: The CBD of AcrVA4 is nestled on the surface of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex wedge (WED) domain.
source: The CBD of AcrVA4 is nestled on the surface of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex wedge (WED) domain and abutted against the recognition 1 (REC1), recognition 2 (REC2) and RuvC domains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: AcrVA4 inserts a glutamate (VA4:E178) to interact with the 5'-hydroxyl of the processed crRNA and a conserved histidine (Cas12a:H759) within the WED domain.
source: AcrVA4 inserts a glutamate (VA4:E178) to interact with the 5'-hydroxyl of the processed crRNA and a conserved histidine (Cas12a:H759) within the WED domain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AcrVA4 E184A and T201A substitutions reduce the inhibition of LbCas12a activity.
source: We observed that both individual AcrVA4 point mutations reduced the inhibition of LbCas12a activity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA cleavage assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: AcrVA4 K202A and E204A mutants display reduced ability to inhibit LbCas12a-catalyzed dsDNA cis-cleavage.
source: To explore the importance of these interactions, we generated K202A and E204A mutants of AcrVA4 and found that they displayed a reduced ability to inhibit LbCas12a-catalyzed dsDNA cis-cleavage (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), consistent with their contributions to the binding interface between Cas12a and AcrVA4 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA cleavage assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: AcrVA4 exploits specific recognition of the pre-crRNA processing nuclease by mimicking the pre-crRNA substrate.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that the bacteriophage-derived AcrVA4 exploits specific recognition of the pre-crRNA processing nuclease by effectively mimicking the pre-crRNA substrate with the contribution of the carboxylates E184 and E204.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical data showing specific interactions.

claim: The CBD of AcrVA4 positions E184 to hydrogen bond with the 5'-hydroxyl on a mature crRNA.
source: Our structure revealed that the CBD of AcrVA4 positions E184 to hydrogen bond with the 5'-hydroxyl on a mature crRNA, termini chemistry generated by Cas12a-catalyzed pre-crRNA cleavage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AcrVA4-mediated inhibition is compromised in the presence of a 5'-PO4 crRNA and lost in the presence of an unprocessable 5'-dT(−21) pre-crRNA.
source: LbCas12a pre-complexed with crRNA bearing a 5'-PO4 or 5'-dT(−21) were still effective at catalyzing dsDNA cis-cleavage; however, AcrVA4-mediated inhibition was compromised in the presence of a 5'-PO4 crRNA and lost in the presence of an unprocessable 5'-dT(−21) pre-crRNA (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA cleavage assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Binding of AcrVA4 to the LbCas12a-crRNA complex is substantially decreased in the presence of crRNA bearing either a 5'-PO4 or 5'-dT(−21).
source: Binding of AcrVA4 to the LbCas12a-crRNA complex was substantially decreased in the presence of crRNA bearing either a 5'-PO4 or 5'-dT(−21), indicative of a binding defect (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: AcrVA4 homodimer assembles with LbCas12a-crRNA into a distribution of two complexes at equilibrium: a monomeric LbCas12a-crRNA bound to the AcrVA4 homodimer and a heterotetrameric assembly.
source: Under our experimental conditions, the AcrVA4 homodimer assembles with LbCas12a-crRNA into a distribution of two complexes at equilibrium: a monomeric LbCas12a-crRNA bound to the AcrVA4 homodimer and a heterotetrameric assembly of two LbCas12a-crRNA complexes bound to an AcrVA4 homodimer (Knott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by previous work and the two states observed in cryo-EM.

claim: A 3D cryo-EM density map at 4.9 Å resolution representing the heterotetrameric State II was reconstructed.
source: Taking a subset of 79,786 particle images identified by 3D classification, we reconstructed a 3D cryo-EM density map at 4.9 Å resolution representing State II (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the cryo-EM experiment.

claim: The two copies of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex in the heterotetramer do not make any direct contacts to each other.
source: Assessing the local environment surrounding the AcrVA4 dimer revealed that the two Cas12a molecules do not make any direct contacts to each other (Figure 3B), suggesting that the interaction between Cas12a and AcrVA4 is due solely to the CBD contact interface.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ɑ1 coiled-coil domain of AcrVA4 projects away from the interface with LbCas12a-crRNA and makes no additional contacts with either Cas12a protomer.
source: Intriguingly, the ɑ1 coiled-coil domain projects away from the interface with LbCas12a-crRNA and makes no additional contacts with either Cas12a protomer.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure of State II.

claim: AcrVA4 blocks dsDNA binding to the LbCas12a-crRNA complex.
source: AcrVA4 blocks dsDNA binding to the LbCas12a-crRNA complex (Knott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited.

claim: AcrVA4 functions through a mode of allosteric, rather than competitive, inhibition.
source: This structural observation suggested that AcrVA4 might function through a mode of allosteric, rather than competitive, inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that AcrVA4 binds away from the DNA binding site.

claim: Inhibitor binding did not change the overall architecture of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex (r.m.s.d = 1.17 Å).
source: To identify the nature of AcrVA4 allosteric control, we superimposed the LbCas12a-crRNA complex (PDB code: 5ID6) on our AcrVA4-bound state revealing that inhibitor binding did not change the overall architecture of the complex (r.m.s.d = 1.17 Å, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is calculated from structural comparison.

claim: A set of subtle distortions to the LbCas12a bridge-helix were observed in the AcrVA4 bound state.
source: Careful inspection of the superimposed states revealed a set of subtle distortions to the LbCas12a bridge-helix in the AcrVA4 bound state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed in the structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The bridge-helix is braced against AcrVA4 where AcrVA4 W178 is stacked against the conserved arginine (LbCas12a: R887).
source: In our structures, the bridge-helix is braced against AcrVA4 (Figure 4A) where AcrVA1 W178 is stacked against the conserved arginine (LbCas12a: R887) with its indole amino proton capping the bridge-helix main chain carbonyl oxygen of Cas12a E885 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: AcrVA4 uses W178 to allosterically lock the bridge-helix to prevent the propagation of conformational changes required to stabilize R-loop formation.
source: The architecture of this interaction suggested that AcrVA4 might use W178 to allosterically lock the bridge-helix to prevent the propagation of conformational changes required to stabilize R-loop formation (Figure 4—video 3) (Swarts et al., 2017; Stella et al., 2017; Stella et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by citations to previous work on Cas12a conformational changes.

claim: AcrVA4-W178A almost completely restored LbCas12a-mediated dsDNA cis-cleavage.
source: To explore the role of W178 we generated AcrVA4-W178A and observed that this substition almost completely restored LbCas12a-mediated dsDNA cis-cleavage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA cleavage assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: AcrVA4-W178A is a dimer able to form a monomeric or heterotetrameric assembly with LbCas12a-crRNA.
source: Using size-exclusion chromatography coupled to di-angle light scattering (SEC-DALS) we determined that, like wild-type AcrVA4, AcrVA4-W178A was itself a dimer (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B) able to form a monomeric or heterotetrameric assembly (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-DALS experiments shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Conformational locking of the LbCas12a bridge-helix by AcrVA4 prevents the dynamics required for R-loop formation.
source: Collectively, these data support a model of allosteric inhibition by AcrVA4 where conformational locking of the LbCas12a bridge-helix prevents the dynamics required for R-loop formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Higher order assembly alone is insufficient to block Cas12a dsDNA targeting.
source: However, LbCas12a-crRNA complexes formed with AcrVA4-W178A can catalyze dsDNA cis-cleavage (Figure 4C). These data suggested that higher order assembly alone was insufficient to block Cas12a dsDNA targeting.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AcrVA4-W178A forms dimers but does not inhibit.

claim: AcrVA4 Δ1–134 exists as a monomer in solution.
source: Using atomistic models (Figure 5A), we generated theoretical SAXS profiles which accurately fit the experimental SAXS data, suggesting that full-length AcrVA4 was dimeric while AcrVA4 Δ1–134 was monomeric in solution (Figure 5B and Table 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-SAXS experiments shown in Figure 5B and Table 2.

claim: AcrVA4 Δ1–134 forms complexes with LbCas12a-crRNA that have 1:1 stoichiometry.
source: Collectively, these results indicated that AcrVA4 Δ1–134 was monomeric and formed complexes with LbCas12a-crRNA that have 1:1 stoichiometry.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-SAXS experiments shown in Figure 5C and Table 2.

claim: AcrVA4 Δ1–134 alone is sufficient to inhibit dsDNA cis-cleavage by LbCas12-crRNA.
source: We observed that AcrVA4 Δ1–134 alone was sufficient to inhibit dsDNA cis-cleavage by LbCas12-crRNA (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA cleavage assays shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of either AcrVA4 or AcrVA4 CBD efficiently inhibits LbCas12a and restores plaquing by the targeted phage.
source: Whereas LbCas12a-crRNA targeting the phage genome confers immunity from lambda infection in E. coli, expression of either AcrVA4 or AcrVA4 CBD efficiently inhibits LbCas12a and restores plaquing by the targeted phage to levels comparable to that observed in the absence of a targeting spacer (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phage plaque assays shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No difference in efficiency of plaquing between full-length and truncated AcrVA4 was observed.
source: Specifically, no difference in efficiency of plaquing between full-length and truncated AcrVA4 was observed, although cells expressing the truncated variant formed smaller plaques (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in phage plaque assays shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The N-terminal domain of AcrVA4 is apparently dispensable for inhibition of LbCas12a both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Furthermore, these data underscore that the N-terminal domain of AcrVA4 is apparently dispensable for inhibition of LbCas12a both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the biochemical and plaque assay data showing that the truncated form is sufficient for inhibition.

claim: AcrVA4 is selective for specific Cas12a enzymes and has no effect on the Cas12a ortholog AsCas12a.
source: In contrast to the broad spectrum inhibition mediated by AcrVA1 (Knott et al., 2019; Watters et al., 2018), AcrVA4 is selective for specific Cas12a enzymes and has no effect on the Cas12a ortholog AsCas12a.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited and experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: AsCas12a contains a helical bundle in the WED domain that forms a compact arrangement proximal to the pre-crRNA processing nuclease.
source: Careful inspection of the LbCas12a-crRNA-AcrVA4 binding interface superimposed onto the available AsCas12a ternary structure revealed the presence of a helical bundle in the AsCas12a WED domain that forms a compact arrangement proximal to the pre-crRNA processing nuclease (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in structural comparison shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The WED domain helical bundle in AsCas12a would sterically clash with AcrVA4.
source: Consistent with this, superimposing the AcrVA4 bound state of LbCas12a-crRNA onto the AsCas12a ternary structure revealed that the WED domain helical bundle would sterically clash with AcrVA4 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is observed in structural comparison shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Chimeric As*Cas12a was robustly inhibited by AcrVA4 while Lb*Cas12a maintained a near wild-type level of dsDNA cis-cleavage.
source: In contrast, the chimeras exhibited a complete phenotype swap where As*Cas12a was robustly inhibited by AcrVA4 while Lb*Cas12a maintained a near wild-type level of dsDNA cis-cleavage (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA cleavage assays shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Removal of the helical bundle rendered As*Cas12a sensitive to AcrVA4, efficiently restoring plaquing of targeted phage.
source: While the chimeric effector maintained the capacity to confer immunity to phage lambda, removal of the helical bundle rendered the enzyme sensitive to AcrVA4, efficiently restoring plaquing of targeted phage to levels consistent with the positive control anti-CRISPR protein (Figure 6D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phage plaque assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Lb#Cas12a achieved complete immunity against phage lambda, even in the presence of AcrVA4.
source: In contrast to Lb*Cas12a, Lb#Cas12a achieved complete immunity against phage lambda, even in the presence of AcrVA4 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phage plaque assays shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Wild-type AsCas12a was not susceptible to AcrVA4 whereas the chimeric enzyme was modestly inhibited in human cell editing experiments.
source: Consistent with our biochemical data, wild-type AsCas12a was not susceptible to AcrVA4 whereas the chimeric enzyme was modestly inhibited from inducing genome edits in the presence of either AcrVA4 or the C-terminal truncated form AcrVA4 Δ1–134 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by human cell editing experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Cas12a orthologs harboring the helical bundle appeared more closely related to TnpB than Cas12a variants lacking the bundle.
source: We found that Cas12a orthologs harboring the helical bundle appeared more closely related to TnpB than Cas12a variants lacking the bundle (Figure 6—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5A.

claim: AsCas12a containing the helical bundle is likely more closely related to a Cas12a common ancestor than LbCas12a which lacks the helical bundle.
source: These observations suggest that AsCas12a containing the helical bundle is likely more closely related to a Cas12a common ancestor than LbCas12a which lacks the helical bundle.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: AcrVA4 is the first example of an anti-CRISPR that exploits recognition of a pre-crRNA processing nuclease.
source: While a number of Acrs have been described that effectively mimic target DNA to block DNA binding, AcrVA4 is the first example of an anti-CRISPR that exploits recognition of a pre-crRNA processing nuclease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data in the context of known Acrs.

claim: The existence of bacteriophage-derived inhibitors targeting the pre-crRNA processing nuclease highlights a unique vulnerability in CRISPR-Cas adaptive immunity.
source: The existence of such bacteriophage-derived inhibitors targeting the pre-crRNA processing nuclease highlights a unique vulnerability in CRISPR-Cas adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is inferred from the discovery of AcrVA4's mechanism.

claim: Other single component effectors that directly catalyze pre-crRNA processing, including Cas13, might also be susceptible to a similar mode of inhibition.
source: Other single component effectors that directly catalyze pre-crRNA processing, including Cas13, might also be susceptible to a similar mode of inhibition, although such Acrs have not yet been identified.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mechanism of AcrVA4.

claim: Dimerization of AcrVA4 and formation of a heterotetrameric interaction with Cas12a is not necessary for inhibition.
source: Although dimerization of AcrVA4 and formation of a heterotetrameric interaction with Cas12a is structurally striking, our biochemical data, phage interference assays, and human gene editing data demonstrated that dimerization is not necessary for inhibition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with the monomeric AcrVA4 Δ1–134.

claim: The N-terminal domain of AcrVA4 may serve an additional function in an endogenous context to provide a selective advantage against activated and trans-cleaving Cas12a.
source: It is possible that the N-terminal domain of AcrVA4 serves an additional function in an endogenous context to provide a selective advantage against activated and trans-cleaving Cas12a.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential function of the N-terminal domain.

claim: Structural variability in divergent Cas12a effectors may be a driver for opportunistic co-evolution of specific bacteriophage inhibitors.
source: Our data also suggest that structural variability in divergent Cas12a effectors may be a driver for opportunistic co-evolution of specific bacteriophage inhibitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic and structural data.

claim: The narrow spectrum of inhibition for AcrVA4 results from the presence of a structural feature in some Cas12a orthologs that occludes inhibitor binding.
source: The narrow spectrum of inhibition for AcrVA4 results from the presence of a structural feature in some Cas12a orthologs that occludes inhibitor binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis and chimeric protein experiments.

claim: The AcrVA4 shield (helical bundle) is ancestral and was lost in a group of Cas12a orthologs after divergence from a common ancestor.
source: Although such a structural elaboration might have been expected to evolve as an insertion to protect Cas12a from Acr targeting, phylogenetic analysis suggested that this AcrVA4 shield is instead ancestral and was lost in a group of Cas12a orthologs after divergence from a common ancestor (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: The fitness advantage driving helical-bundle deletion created the co-evolutionary opportunity by exposing an exploitable site on Cas12a.
source: These data suggest that the fitness advantage driving helical-bundle deletion created the co-evolutionary opportunity by exposing an exploitable site on Cas12a.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic and structural data.

claim: Bacteria might avoid anti-CRISPR activity by accommodating indels that do not interfere with activity but provide steric protection from Acr association.
source: In this way, bacteria might avoid anti-CRISPR activity by accommodating indels that do not interfere with activity but provide steric protection from Acr association.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: This process could help explain the prevalence of large indels seemingly scattered at random throughout CRISPR-Cas effectors and the diversification of CRISPR systems leading to anti-CRISPR resistence.
source: Such a process could help explain the prevalence of large indels seemingly scattered at random throughout CRISPR-Cas effectors and the diversification of CRISPR systems leading to anti-CRISPR resistence (Pausch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The limited spectrum of inhibition available to some anti-CRISPRs might be expanded by protein engineering.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the limited spectrum of inhibition available to some anti-CRISPRs might be expanded by protein engineering, effectively reprogramming anti-CRISPR susceptibilities.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful engineering of chimeric Cas12a proteins.

claim: Cas12a cleaves DNA following recognition of a 20-nucleotide DNA sequence containing a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM).
source: Cas12a (formerly Cpf1) is an RNA-guided Class II type V-A CRISPR nuclease which cleaves DNA following recognition of a 20-nucleotide DNA sequence containing a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) (Zetsche et al., 2015) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Previously identified inhibitors of Cas12a either reversibly block substrate association through stoichiometric binding or irreversibly inactivate the enzyme complex through a chemical transformation.
source: Previously identified inhibitors of Cas12a, known as type V-A Acrs (AcrVA), either reversibly block substrate association through stoichiometric binding or irreversibly inactivate the enzyme complex through a chemical transformation (Suresh et al., 2019; Knott et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AcrVA4 exhibits stoichiometric inhibition of Cas12a.
source: While exhibiting stoichiometric inhibition of Cas12a, the inhibitor AcrVA4 appears to be unique in several ways.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of AcrVA4.

claim: AcrVA4 blocks dsDNA binding to L. bacterium (Lb) and M. bovoculi (Mb) Cas12a but not Ac. species (As) Cas12a.
source: Previous biochemical experiments demonstrated that AcrVA4 blocks dsDNA binding to L. bacterium (Lb) and M. bovoculi (Mb) Cas12a but not Ac. species (As) Cas12a (Watters et al., 2018; Knott et al., 2019), the last of which is commonly utilized as a tool for genome editing (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AsCas12a is commonly utilized as a tool for genome editing.
source: Previous biochemical experiments demonstrated that AcrVA4 blocks dsDNA binding to L. bacterium (Lb) and M. bovoculi (Mb) Cas12a but not Ac. species (As) Cas12a (Watters et al., 2018; Knott et al., 2019), the last of which is commonly utilized as a tool for genome editing (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: To recognize dsDNA, Cas12a binds a TTTV PAM sequence via the PAM-interacting (PI) domain, triggering crRNA strand invasion and base-pairing with the target strand.
source: To recognize dsDNA, Cas12a binds a TTTV PAM sequence via the PAM-interacting (PI) domain, triggering crRNA strand invasion and base-pairing with the target strand (Nishimasu et al., 2017; Swarts et al., 2017; Yamano et al., 2016; Nishimasu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: LbCas12a must undergo a large conformational change to form a stable R-loop structure upon DNA binding.
source: To form a stable R-loop structure upon DNA binding, LbCas12a must undergo a large conformational change (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 4—video 1.

claim: The movement of the LbCas12a bridge-helix drives a conserved arginine residue, R887, towards the cRNA: DNA heteroduplex.
source: Significant among these domain motions is the movement of the LbCas12a bridge-helix which drives a conserved arginine residue, R887, towards the cRNA: DNA heteroduplex (Figure 4—video 2) (Yamano et al., 2016; Yamano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and shown in Figure 4—video 2.

claim: Both chimeric enzymes (As*Cas12a and Lb*Cas12a) exhibited modest (~five fold) reductions in the rate of pre-crRNA processing.
source: Both chimeric enzymes (As*Cas12a and Lb*Cas12a) exhibited modest (~five fold) reductions in the rate of pre-crRNA processing (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B) but maintained near wild-type dsDNA cis-cleavage activity in the absence of AcrVA4 (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pre-crRNA processing assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Both chimeric enzymes maintained near wild-type dsDNA cis-cleavage activity in the absence of AcrVA4.
source: Both chimeric enzymes (As*Cas12a and Lb*Cas12a) exhibited modest (~five fold) reductions in the rate of pre-crRNA processing (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B) but maintained near wild-type dsDNA cis-cleavage activity in the absence of AcrVA4 (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA cleavage assays shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.
